To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the policies have a negative impact on the probability of college attendance and completion; (ii) they have a positive impact on the probability that a student will be employed and on the probability of being employed full‐time; and (iii) the impact of the policies on the probability of attending college is greater among students who are not vocational concentrators.
the policies’ emphasis on academics is not necessarily a bad thing for vocational concentrators.
raising academic standards and introducing the Minimum Competency Examination are good policies for the economy as a whole but bad policies for vocational concentrators.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of high school reforms on the post‐secondary outcomes of vocational concentrators.
the effects of the academic standards movement on students who are less likely to be affected by it.
the effects of high school graduation requirements on the postsecondary education and labor market outcomes of vocational concentrators.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of these policies on students are positive, but not as large as the effects on the labor market.
the policies’ emphasis on academic standards and the introduction of a Minimum Competency Exam have positive impacts on labor market outcomes, but they reduce college attendance and completion.
raising academic standards in high school has a negative effect on college attendance and completion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
raising academic standards is good for the economy, but not for the students.
raising academic standards and vocational concentrations are complementary policies that improve the labor market outcomes of high school graduates.
the new policies have a positive effect for vocational concentrators, while the negative effects for non‐concentrates are not large.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the academic standards reforms of the last decades have been a success for all types of students, but particularly for those who are less likely to go to college.
the effects of academic standards are heterogeneous and depend on the type of student.
policymakers should not be afraid of requiring more academic courses to graduate from high school.
